title: 05 — Microsoft Entra ID & Identity for .NET Developers
html:
05 — Microsoft Entra ID & Identity for .NET Developers

Entra ID is the renamed Azure Active Directory (renamed 2023 — the API, the SDKs and half the documentation still say "AAD", and login.microsoftonline.com is unchanged). This is the most valuable Azure file for a .NET developer: identity is how everything else authenticates.

1. The objects, and how they relate

flowchart TB
    subgraph Tenant["Entra ID tenant (your directory)"]
      U[Users] --> G[Groups]
      AR["App registration<br/>(the GLOBAL definition of an app:<br/>redirect URIs, scopes, roles, secrets)"]
      SP["Service principal / Enterprise application<br/>(the LOCAL identity of that app in THIS tenant:<br/>consent, role assignments, sign-in logs)"]
      AR -->|creates one per tenant| SP
      MI["Managed identity<br/>(a service principal Azure creates and<br/>manages for you — NO credentials)"]
    end
    SP --> RBAC[Azure RBAC role assignments]
    MI --> RBAC
    G --> RBAC
Object What it is You use it for
App registration The application's definition: client ID, redirect URIs, exposed scopes, app roles, credentials Registering your API and your SPA
Service principal (shown as "Enterprise application") The application's identity in a specific tenant RBAC assignments, consent, sign-in audit
Managed identity A service principal Azure creates, and whose credentials Azure rotates for you ⭐ Everything running in Azure
Workload identity federation Trust an external OIDC issuer (GitHub, Azure DevOps, another cloud) instead of a secret ⭐ CI/CD pipelines

The distinction that gets asked: an app registration is the global blueprint; a service principal is the instance of it in a tenant. A multi-tenant app has one registration in the publisher's tenant and a service principal in every customer's tenant.

2. ⭐ Managed identity — the single most important concept

What it solves: your app needs to call Key Vault, Storage, SQL, Service Bus. Traditionally that means a connection string or a client secret — which must be stored, rotated, and inevitably leaks. A managed identity is an Entra identity that Azure creates and whose credentials Azure rotates automatically. Your code never sees a credential.

2.1 System-assigned vs user-assigned

System-assigned User-assigned
Lifecycle Created with the resource, deleted with it Independent resource; survives the app
Shared One resource only Many resources can share one identity
RBAC setup Must be re-granted if the resource is recreated Granted once, stable
Use when A single app with its own permissions ⭐ Multiple apps/slots sharing a permission set, or IaC where you want the identity to exist before the app

💡 Recommendation: user-assigned for anything managed by IaC. The system-assigned identity's principal ID changes if the resource is recreated, which breaks every role assignment and forces a re-grant. A user-assigned identity lets you create the identity, grant it, and then attach it to the app — the ordering IaC wants.

⚠️ A deployment slot has its own managed identity. If you grant Key Vault access to the production app but not the staging slot, the app works after a swap and fails before it — a genuinely confusing failure.

2.2 How it works underneath

App Service / Function / VM / Container App
   │  (1) HTTP GET http://169.254.169.254/metadata/identity/oauth2/token
   │      ?resource=https://vault.azure.net   (+ a header with a secret injected by the platform)
   ▼
Azure Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) — a link-local endpoint only reachable from inside the VM
   │  (2) returns a short-lived access token for the managed identity
   ▼
Your code calls Key Vault with  Authorization: Bearer <token>

DefaultAzureCredential does this for you and caches the token. ⚠️ The IMDS endpoint is why SSRF is dangerous in Azure — a server-side request forgery that reaches 169.254.169.254 can steal your app's identity token. See 13_SECURITY_ENGINEERING in the main KB.

2.3 Using it in .NET

// Program.cs — one credential, used by every Azure client
var credential = new DefaultAzureCredential(new DefaultAzureCredentialOptions
{
    // In Azure this resolves to the managed identity; locally to your az login / VS account
    ManagedIdentityClientId = builder.Configuration["Azure:UserAssignedClientId"],  // if user-assigned
    ExcludeVisualStudioCredential   = !builder.Environment.IsDevelopment(),
    ExcludeAzurePowerShellCredential = !builder.Environment.IsDevelopment(),
    ExcludeInteractiveBrowserCredential = true
});

builder.Services.AddAzureClients(clients =>
{
    clients.UseCredential(credential);
    clients.AddSecretClient(new Uri(builder.Configuration["KeyVaultUri"]!));
    clients.AddBlobServiceClient(new Uri(builder.Configuration["StorageUri"]!));
    clients.AddServiceBusClientWithNamespace(builder.Configuration["ServiceBusNamespace"]!);
});

Azure SQL with a managed identity — no password anywhere:

// Connection string with NO credentials
"Server=tcp:sql-shop-prod.database.windows.net,1433;Database=shop;
 Authentication=Active Directory Default;Encrypt=True;TrustServerCertificate=False;"

-- Run ONCE in the database, connected as an Entra admin
CREATE USER [app-shop-api-prod] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER;   -- the managed identity's name
ALTER ROLE db_datareader ADD MEMBER [app-shop-api-prod];
ALTER ROLE db_datawriter ADD MEMBER [app-shop-api-prod];
-- ⚠️ Do NOT add it to db_owner. Grant EXECUTE on specific schemas if it needs procedures.

⚠️ Two gotchas: the SQL user must be created by an Entra administrator on the server (not a SQL login), and for a user-assigned identity you must also set the client ID so the driver requests the right token.

3. Workload identity federation (for pipelines and non-Azure workloads)

Covered operationally in files 02 and 03. The concept: instead of a secret, Entra ID trusts an external OIDC issuer and validates the token's iss + sub claims against a federated identity credential you configure.

GitHub Actions token:      sub = repo:my-org/my-repo:environment:production
Azure DevOps token:        sub = sc://myorg/myproject/sc-azure-prod
Kubernetes (AKS) token:    sub = system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<serviceaccount>

💡 This is how you eliminate the last secret. A mature Azure estate has zero stored client secrets: managed identity inside Azure, federation for everything outside it.

4. OAuth 2.0 and OIDC — the flows you need

Flow Use Notes
Authorization Code + PKCE ⭐ Web apps, SPAs, mobile — the only flow for user sign-in PKCE binds the code to the client that started the flow
Client credentials Service-to-service (daemon, background job) No user. Prefer managed identity where the caller is in Azure
On-Behalf-Of (OBO) API A calls API B as the signed-in user Preserves per-user authorisation downstream
Device code CLI, TV, no browser on the device
❌ Implicit — Deprecated. Tokens in the URL fragment
❌ Resource Owner Password — Deprecated. The app sees the user's password

4.1 The tokens

Token For Contains Validate?
ID token The client — "who signed in" sub, name, email, nonce Yes, by the client
Access token The API — "what may be done" aud, scp (delegated scopes), roles (app roles), oid, tid ⭐ Yes, by the API
Refresh token Getting new access tokens without re-authenticating Opaque Never sent to an API

⚠️ An API must validate the access token, never the ID token. An ID token's audience is the client, not your API — accepting one is an authentication bypass. This is a real vulnerability class and a common review finding.

4.2 Delegated permissions (scp) vs application permissions (roles)

Delegated (scp) Application (roles)
Acting as The signed-in user (the app can never exceed the user's own rights) The app itself, no user
Consent User or admin Admin only
Token claim scp: "Portfolio.Read Portfolio.Write" roles: ["Portfolio.ReadAll"]
Use for Interactive apps Daemons, background jobs

⚠️ Application permissions are dangerous — Portfolio.ReadAll means all portfolios, with no user context to constrain it. Grant them sparingly and audit them.

5. Protecting an ASP.NET Core API

builder.Services.AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApi(builder.Configuration.GetSection("AzureAd"));

// Deny by default; opt out explicitly with [AllowAnonymous]
builder.Services.AddAuthorizationBuilder()
    .SetFallbackPolicy(new AuthorizationPolicyBuilder().RequireAuthenticatedUser().Build())
    .AddPolicy("PortfolioRead", p => p.RequireAssertion(ctx =>
        ctx.User.HasScope("Portfolio.Read") || ctx.User.IsInRole("Portfolio.ReadAll")));

// appsettings.json — no secrets here
{
  "AzureAd": {
    "Instance": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/",
    "TenantId": "<tenant-guid>",
    "ClientId": "<api-app-registration-client-id>",   // this API's OWN app registration
    "Audience": "api://<api-client-id>"
  }
}

What AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApi validates for you — and what you should be able to list:

  1. Signature against the tenant's published JWKS (keys are fetched and cached from the OIDC metadata endpoint).
  2. Issuer (iss) matches the expected tenant.
  3. Audience (aud) is this API.
  4. Lifetime (exp, nbf) with a small clock skew.
  5. Algorithm — pin it. ⚠️ alg: none and RS256/HS256 confusion are real attack classes.
// Reading the caller's identity correctly
var objectId = User.GetObjectId();                 // `oid` — STABLE per user per tenant
var tenantId = User.GetTenantId();                 // `tid`
var email    = User.FindFirst("preferred_username")?.Value;

⚠️ Use oid (+ tid) as the user key in your database, not email or UPN. Email addresses change when people marry, get renamed, or move domain — and sub is pairwise (different per application), so it's not portable across your own services.

6. Calling a downstream API on behalf of the user (OBO)

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant SPA as Angular SPA
    participant A as Your API
    participant D as Downstream API (e.g. Graph)
    U->>SPA: sign in (Auth Code + PKCE)
    SPA->>A: GET /portfolios  Bearer <token for YOUR api>
    A->>A: validate token
    A->>Entra: OBO exchange:<br/>my token + client credential → token for D
    Entra-->>A: access token for D, still carrying the user's identity
    A->>D: GET /me/messages  Bearer <token for D>

builder.Services.AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApiAuthentication(builder.Configuration)
    .EnableTokenAcquisitionToCallDownstreamApi()
    .AddMicrosoftGraph(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Graph"))
    .AddInMemoryTokenCaches();      // ⚠️ use a DISTRIBUTED cache in a multi-instance app

public class PortfolioController(GraphServiceClient graph) : ControllerBase
{
    [HttpGet("me")]
    [RequiredScope("User.Read")]
    public async Task<IActionResult> Me(CancellationToken ct)
        => Ok(await graph.Me.GetAsync(cancellationToken: ct));
}

⚠️ AddInMemoryTokenCaches in a scaled-out app means a cache miss on every instance — more round trips to Entra and possible throttling. Use AddDistributedTokenCaches backed by Redis in production.

💡 Prefer OBO over dropping to the app's own identity. If your API calls a downstream service as itself, you lose per-user authorisation and every audit log downstream shows the service, not the person.

7. Securing an Angular SPA (MSAL)

// The SPA gets its OWN app registration, configured as a "Single-page application" platform
export const msalConfig: Configuration = {
  auth: {
    clientId: environment.spaClientId,
    authority: `https://login.microsoftonline.com/${environment.tenantId}`,
    redirectUri: environment.redirectUri,
  },
  cache: {
    cacheLocation: 'sessionStorage',   // 💡 sessionStorage over localStorage: smaller XSS window
    storeAuthStateInCookie: false,
  },
};

// Attach the token only to YOUR API — never send your API's token to a third party
export const protectedResourceMap = new Map<string, Array<string>>([
  [environment.apiBaseUrl, [`api://${environment.apiClientId}/Portfolio.Read`]],
]);

Setup facts:

  • The SPA registration must use the SPA platform type (which enables PKCE and the CORS-enabled token endpoint), not "Web" — a "Web" platform expects a client secret, which a browser cannot keep.
  • The SPA requests a scope exposed by the API registration (api://<api-client-id>/Portfolio.Read), not its own client ID.
  • ⚠️ Tokens in localStorage/sessionStorage are readable by any XSS. The most secure pattern is the Backend-for-Frontend: the SPA holds no token; a server-side session cookie (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite) fronts the API. More plumbing, materially better security posture.

8. App roles, groups, and authorisation models

Mechanism Where defined Token claim Notes
App roles On the app registration roles ⭐ Application-specific, portable, doesn't depend on directory structure
Group membership Entra groups groups ⚠️ Overage: beyond ~200 groups the claim is replaced by a Graph link, and naive code silently sees no groups
Custom claims Claims mapping policy / extension attributes custom Advanced
Local authorisation Your database — Roles/permissions your app owns

💡 Recommendation: define app roles for coarse access ("Analyst", "Approver") and keep fine-grained, resource-level authorisation in your own domain (who owns which portfolio). Directory groups are for organisational membership, not for expressing your application's permission model.

// App role in the manifest → a `roles` claim → policy-based authorisation
[Authorize(Roles = "Portfolio.Approver")]
[HttpPost("{id}/approve")]
public async Task<IActionResult> Approve(Guid id, CancellationToken ct) { ... }

⚠️ A token issued before a role change still carries the old roles until it expires. For sensitive operations, check authority against the source of truth at the time of the action, not only the token claim.

9. Conditional Access and MFA (what a developer needs to know)

Conditional Access is a policy engine: if (user/group, app, device state, location, risk) then (block, require MFA, require compliant device, limit session).

Why a developer cares:

  • Your app may receive an interaction_required / AADSTS50076 error when a CA policy demands step-up MFA mid-flow. Handle it by triggering an interactive re-authentication with the returned claims challenge — don't just show "login failed".
  • Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) can revoke a token mid-lifetime (user disabled, network location change). CAE-aware apps must handle a 401 with a claims challenge and retry, rather than treating it as a hard failure.
  • Device/location policies can break service-to-service calls if a workload accidentally falls under a user policy — a reason to keep workload identities distinct.

10. Local development

az login                      # DefaultAzureCredential picks this up
az account set --subscription "My Dev Subscription"
Environment What DefaultAzureCredential resolves to
Your machine Azure CLI / Visual Studio / VS Code account
GitHub Actions Workload identity federation
App Service, Functions, Container Apps, AKS, VM Managed identity

Give your own developer account the same data-plane roles the app's managed identity has in dev (Key Vault Secrets User, Storage Blob Data Contributor). Then the same code path runs locally and in Azure with zero configuration difference — that's the entire value of DefaultAzureCredential.

⚠️ Never use a service principal secret for local development "because it's easier". It leaks into .env files, screenshots, and eventually the repository.

11. Troubleshooting identity

Error Cause
AADSTS700016 — application not found in directory Wrong tenant, or the app registration is in a different tenant
AADSTS50011 — redirect URI mismatch The URI must match exactly, including trailing slash and scheme
AADSTS65001 — user or admin has not consented Grant admin consent, or the app must prompt for it
AADSTS500011 — resource principal not found The API's service principal doesn't exist in this tenant, or the audience is wrong
401 with a valid-looking token Wrong aud — you're probably sending the ID token instead of the access token
403 after granting Contributor You need the data-plane role (Key Vault Secrets User, Storage Blob Data Contributor…)
Managed identity works in prod, not in a slot The slot has its own identity — grant it separately
ManagedIdentityCredential authentication failed locally Expected — there's no IMDS on your laptop; DefaultAzureCredential should fall through to the CLI credential
Token has no groups claim Group overage — read groups from Graph, or use app roles instead

🧪 Decode a token and check the claims — paste it into jwt.ms (Microsoft's decoder; it doesn't transmit the token). Check aud, iss, scp/roles, oid, tid, exp.

12. Checklist

  • Zero client secrets. Managed identity inside Azure, federation for pipelines
  • User-assigned managed identity where IaC manages the lifecycle
  • Deployment slots granted their own RBAC
  • Data-plane roles granted (not just Contributor)
  • API validates the access token: issuer, audience, lifetime, signature, pinned algorithm
  • Deny-by-default authorisation with a fallback policy
  • oid + tid used as the user key, never email
  • Scopes/app roles defined and checked per endpoint
  • SPA uses the SPA platform type with PKCE; token storage risk understood (BFF if the data is sensitive)
  • Distributed token cache in multi-instance apps
  • OBO used when calling downstream APIs on a user's behalf
  • Conditional Access claims challenges handled, not swallowed
  • Developer accounts have the same dev-environment data roles as the app

🔍 Questions to test yourself

  • App registration vs service principal vs managed identity? Global definition / per-tenant identity / an Azure-managed service principal with no credentials you handle.
  • System-assigned vs user-assigned managed identity? Tied to the resource lifecycle vs independent and shareable; prefer user-assigned under IaC because the principal ID stays stable.
  • How does a managed identity get a token? The platform exposes IMDS on a link-local address; the SDK requests a token for the target resource and caches it. (And that's why SSRF to 169.254.169.254 is dangerous.)
  • Delegated vs application permissions? Acting as the user, constrained by their rights vs acting as the app with no user context — admin consent only, and far more dangerous.
  • Why must an API validate the access token and not the ID token? The ID token's audience is the client; accepting it bypasses authentication.
  • How do you call Microsoft Graph as the signed-in user from your API? On-Behalf-Of flow, with a distributed token cache.

Sources: Managed identities for Azure resources — Microsoft Learn · Managed identities in App Service · Access Azure databases with managed identity · Managed identity developer introduction
